facts.fact_text: On 27 September 2013 a group of LGBTI rights activists informed the St Petersburg authorities of their intention to hold a meeting to mark Coming Out Day (an annual LGBTI awareness day).
The meeting to mark Coming Out Day was planned to take place from 2 p.m. until 3.30 p.m. on 12 October 2013.
The meeting to mark Coming Out Day was planned to be held at the Field of Mars (Марсово поле), a large square in the city centre of St Petersburg.
About 150 people were expected to attend the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
At about 1 p.m. on 12 October 2013 the applicant arrived at the Field of Mars to take part in the preparation of the Coming Out Day meeting.

According to the applicant, the Coming Out Day participants (about twenty or thirty people) were unable to gather at the Field of Mars because the place was blocked by more than 100 aggressive counter-demonstrators.

According to the applicant, the Coming Out Day participants (about twenty or thirty people) were unable to gather at the Field of Mars because the place was blocked by more than 100 aggressive counter-demonstrators.
According to the applicant, the Coming Out Day participants asked for help from the police officers present at the Field of Mars, but the police officers did not react.
At 1.55 p.m. on 12 October 2013 police officers surrounded a group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, Mr D.G., Mr D.M., Ms N.I., Ms E.M., Ms S.L. and Ms Y.T.
The police officers stated that the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, had breached public order by using foul language in a public place.
The police officers ordered the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, to proceed to a police bus.

The police officers took the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, to central police station no. 28 in St Petersburg (28 отдел полиции УМВД России по центральному району г. Санкт-Петербургу).

The police officers referred to the transfer procedure set out in Article 27.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences as the legal basis for taking the demonstrators to central police station no. 28 in St Petersburg.

The relevant provisions of the Code of Administrative Offences, including Article 27.2 ('Transfer procedure') and Article 27.3 ('Administrative detention'), are summarised in Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia (no. 76204/11, § 44, 4 December 2014).
The police officers stated that the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, had breached public order by using foul language in a public place.

The administrative-offence record specified that the grounds of the applicant's arrest were that she had used foul language during the public meeting and had ignored warnings given by police officers to refrain from doing so.
The police deployed around 540 police officers, including officers from special-purpose units, to ensure public order during the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
The enhanced security deployment of approximately 540 police officers was ordered in the light of anticipated clashes with counter-demonstrators.
According to the applicant, the Coming Out Day participants asked for help from the police officers present at the Field of Mars, but the police officers did not react.
According to the applicant, the police officers at the Field of Mars stepped in only when counter-demonstrators insulted the police officers personally.
According to the applicant, the police officers arrested several counter-demonstrators, took them to a police bus parked nearby, and then released them.
According to the applicant, the released counter-demonstrators continued their verbal attacks and physical pressure on the LGBTI activists present at the Field of Mars.

The police officers stated that the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, had breached public order by using foul language in a public place.
The police officers ordered the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, to proceed to a police bus.

The police officers took the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, to central police station no. 28 in St Petersburg (28 отдел полиции УМВД России по центральному району г. Санкт-Петербургу).
The Government submitted that in total, ninety-three people had been arrested during the public event on 12 October 2013 on account of their disorderly conduct.
The applicant argued that the police officers had taken only participants in the Coming Out Day meeting to various police stations on 12 October 2013.

Relying on a video recording of the event of 12 October 2013, the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg established that the police had interfered with the public gathering because of the conflict between the demonstrators and counter-demonstrators.

The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg found on 23 October 2014 that the applicant had been one of the active participants in the conflict between demonstrators and counter-demonstrators on 12 October 2013.
The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg concluded on 23 October 2014 that the applicant's arrest had been lawful.

The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg was not convinced by witness evidence stating that the applicant herself had not breached public order, because the witnesses belonged to the same group of demonstrators as the applicant.

The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg concluded on 23 October 2014 that the applicant's detention had been lawful, as its duration had not exceeded forty-eight hours, the maximum length of administrative detention provided by Article 27.5 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg found on 23 October 2014 that the applicant's allegation regarding the authorities' failure to ensure the personal safety of the demonstrators had been unsubstantiated by evidence.
The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg noted on 23 October 2014 that about 550 police officers had been deployed by the authorities during the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg noted on 23 October 2014 that no harm had been caused to the applicant during the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
In her appeal of 31 December 2014, the applicant alleged that no counter-demonstrators had been detained during the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
In her appeal of 31 December 2014, the applicant alleged that the selective approach of arresting only Coming Out Day participants and not counter-demonstrators had been discriminatory.

On 31 March 2010, at the 1081st meeting of Ministers' Deputies, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe adopted Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 on measures to combat discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe provides that member states should take appropriate measures at national, regional and local levels to ensure that the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, as enshrined in Article 11 of the Convention, can be effectively enjoyed without discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe provides that member states should ensure that law enforcement authorities take appropriate measures to protect participants in peaceful demonstrations in favour of the human rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons from any attempts to unlawfully disrupt or inhibit the effective enjoyment of their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that the duty to protect involves the protection of assembly organizers and participants from third party individuals or groups who seek to undermine their right to freedom of peaceful assembly.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that state authorities must protect the organizers and participants of peaceful assemblies that espouse controversial or unpopular views from hostile opposition, and shall protect peaceful assemblies from any person or group that intentionally seeks to limit or destroy the rights of others to assemble.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that potential disorder arising from hostility directed against those participating in a peaceful assembly must not be used to justify disproportionate restrictions on the assembly.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that the state should take positive measures to facilitate assemblies associated with individuals and groups that have historically faced discrimination, or are otherwise marginalized or at risk.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that law enforcement officials must differentiate between peaceful and non-peaceful participants, since only those who themselves take part in violence forfeit the legal guarantee of their right to assemble, and that state intervention should target individual wrongdoers rather than all participants more generally.

In a report entitled 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia' published in December 2014, the NGO Human Rights Watch stated that since at least the mid-2000s, Russian authorities had refused to tolerate most public events in support of LGBT rights and equality.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch stated that homophobic counter-demonstrators had violently disrupted many public events in support of LGBT rights and equality in Russia.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch stated that the vast majority of people it interviewed who had been involved in such events said that the frequency of attacks had risen over the previous two years.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch stated that in 2013 anti-gay activists had attacked virtually every LGBT equality event of which Human Rights Watch were aware.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch described how anti-gay counter-protesters routinely harassed LGBT activists and their supporters during public events, used offensive homophobic slurs, or threatened them with physical violence.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch stated that in five out of seven cases documented in the report, police had not taken adequate measures to prevent and stop the harassment and attacks.

One of the five cases in which police had not taken adequate measures to prevent and stop harassment and attacks, as documented in the December 2014 Human Rights Watch report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', concerned the public meeting of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.
A Human Rights Watch researcher observed the Coming Out Day rally organized by LGBT activists on 12 October 2013 at the Field of Mars in central St Petersburg.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, after about a dozen LGBT activists arrived at the Field of Mars for the Coming Out Day rally on 12 October 2013, a crowd of at least five times as many anti-gay counter-protesters harassed and attacked them.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, some of the counter-protesters at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 were dressed as priests with religious accessories; others were in military uniforms and camouflage outfits.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the counter-protesters at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 yelled that gays were 'abnormal' and that there was no place for them in St Petersburg, and blocked access for LGBT activists to the protest venue.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, after several attempts to reach the venue at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013, the LGBT activists were unable to start the Coming Out Day event.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the LGBT activists told the police at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 that they were effectively barred from reaching the event venue.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the police at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013, who numbered several dozen ordinary police officers and many riot police, did not take adequate measures to ensure access to the venue and prevent harassment and attacks by anti-gay counter-protesters.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the police at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 began detaining counter-protesters only when several of them started insulting police officers for not stopping the LGBT rally.
According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, a few LGBT activists were also detained at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 but were released after several hours.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the initial charges against the detained LGBT activists of organizing and participating in an unsanctioned public event were eventually dropped.

On an unspecified date after 12 February 2014, the applicant extended her civil claim, alleging that the authorities had failed to ensure the personal safety of the participants in the public meeting of 12 October 2013.

The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg found on 23 October 2014 that the applicant's allegation regarding the authorities' failure to ensure the personal safety of the demonstrators had been unsubstantiated by evidence.
